vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the pharmacy's climate-controlled backroom, mechanically counting tablets into amber bottles. His hands move with practiced efficiency—a skill he's honed across three years of university and two years working at Westfield Pharmacy. But his mind isn't on the medications. It's on his younger brother, Daniel, and the night that changed everything.

Eight months ago, Marcus was home alone when the phone call came. Daniel had been hit by a drunk driver while crossing the street near the university campus. Marcus remembers the exact words the police officer used: "serious injuries," "critical condition," "get to the hospital now." The drive there felt endless, though it was only fifteen minutes. Marcus's hands shook so badly he nearly missed the exit twice.

Daniel spent forty-three days in the intensive care unit. Marcus was there for most of them, sitting in the plastic chair beside his brother's bed, watching the ventilator inflate and deflate, counting the machines that kept him alive. Daniel survived, but the recovery has been long and incomplete. He's regained consciousness, but he has a traumatic brain injury. Some days are better than others. Some days, Daniel doesn't recognize Marcus at all.

Since then, Marcus has changed in ways he doesn't fully understand. He still goes to work—he has to, his family needs the income—but the pharmacy feels different now. The fluorescent lights seem too bright, almost hostile. When a customer approaches the counter suddenly, Marcus's heart rate spikes. His body tenses, waiting for bad news. He's learned to hide it, to smile and answer questions about drug interactions and side effects, but internally, he's bracing himself for disaster.

Driving has become nearly impossible. Marcus takes the bus to work now, though it adds forty minutes to his commute. Every time he gets behind the wheel, he sees the intersection where Daniel was hit. He imagines the impact, the sound of breaking glass, Daniel's body flying. Logically, Marcus knows his brother wasn't hit in his car. But his nervous system doesn't seem to care about logic. His hands sweat. His breathing becomes shallow. After two near-misses—moments where he wasn't paying attention—he decided the bus was safer for everyone.

Sleep is fragmented. Marcus lies awake most nights, his mind replaying the hospital waiting room, the machines beeping, the doctor's expression when she said Daniel's prognosis was uncertain. When he does sleep, he has vivid nightmares—sometimes about the accident itself, sometimes about Daniel dying despite everyone's efforts. He wakes gasping, sheets soaked with sweat. He's started drinking a beer or two before bed, hoping it will help him sleep through the night. It doesn't really work, but he does it anyway.

At the pharmacy, Marcus has become hyper-focused on safety protocols. He checks and rechecks medications, sometimes three or four times, terrified of making an error that could harm someone. His manager has noticed his increased attention to detail, but what she doesn't see is the anxiety underneath it—the belief that if he can just control everything perfectly in this one space, maybe he can prevent another tragedy.

His coworkers think he's just dedicated. His parents think he's coping well because he hasn't fallen apart. But Marcus knows the truth: he's functioning, but he's not living. He's going through the motions of his life while existing in a state of constant vigilance, waiting for the next disaster, convinced that safety is an illusion and that everyone he loves is fragile in ways he can't protect against.
